mcqs.question: Why can't a compulsory (cold) miss be eliminated even by an infinitely large, fully associative cache?
options: Because infinite caches still have a fixed replacement policy
Because the block was never in cache before, so no placement or capacity policy can prevent the very first access from missing
Because compulsory misses only occur in direct-mapped caches
Because fully associative caches don't support compulsory misses by design
mcqs.explanation: Compulsory misses are about timing, not cache shape or size — the very first reference to a block has nothing to hit against yet, no matter how large or associative the cache is. They occur in every cache type, and the only real mitigation is prefetching the data before it's needed.

mcqs.question: How can you tell a capacity miss apart from a conflict miss when diagnosing a cache?
options: Capacity misses only happen on the first access; conflict misses happen on every access
A capacity miss would still occur even in a fully associative cache of the same size; a conflict miss would not
Capacity misses only occur in write-back caches
There's no way to distinguish them; the terms are interchangeable
mcqs.explanation: The defining test is whether a fully associative cache of the same total size would also take the miss. If yes, the working set genuinely doesn't fit (capacity); if a fully associative cache would have avoided it, it was purely a placement collision (conflict). Write policy is unrelated to this distinction.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a coherence miss from the original 3 Cs (compulsory, capacity, conflict)?
options: Coherence misses are caused by another core writing to a shared address, not by this core's own access pattern or the local cache's shape
Coherence misses only occur in direct-mapped caches
Coherence misses are just a renamed version of conflict misses
Coherence misses can be eliminated entirely by increasing associativity
mcqs.explanation: The 3 Cs are all explained by a single core's own access pattern versus its cache's size and shape. Coherence misses are fundamentally different — they're forced by another core's write invalidating this core's copy, a cross-core phenomenon that more associativity or a bigger cache cannot fix.

mcqs.question: You simulate a workload's miss rate as associativity increases from 1-way to 8-way at fixed total cache size, and the miss rate barely changes. What does that suggest?
options: The misses are dominated by conflict misses, so more associativity should have helped
The misses are dominated by capacity misses — the working set doesn't fit regardless of how placement is arranged
The cache has a hardware defect
The workload has no compulsory misses at all
mcqs.explanation: If more placement freedom (higher associativity) doesn't reduce misses, the problem isn't collisions between blocks fighting for the same set — it's that the working set is simply too big for this cache size at any associativity, which is the signature of capacity misses. Compulsory misses are still present regardless; they just aren't what this experiment is measuring.
